article.overview: A thermal emission spectrometer measures the infrared radiation that a planetary surface emits because of its own temperature, and separates that radiation into wavelengths. The shape of the resulting spectrum depends on surface temperature, composition and grain structure, so it can help identify rock-forming minerals and fine-grained silicate materials [3][4]. Because it relies on emitted heat rather than reflected sunlight, it complements reflectance spectroscopy and can be used at night [3]. No thermal emission spectrometer is reported in the sources reviewed as operating in lunar orbit or on the lunar surface. The lunar examples are a 2022 flyby observation by the Lucy spacecraft and the Lunar Thermal Mapper, an instrument built for NASA's Lunar Trailblazer mission that was lost after its 2025 launch [4][6][7].
article.description: A thermal emission spectrometer records the spectrum of infrared energy leaving a surface, usually in the thermal infrared. The Mars Global Surveyor Thermal Emission Spectrometer (TES) used an interferometric spectrometer covering 5.8 to 50 micrometres, with additional broadband thermal and visible/near-infrared radiometers [1]. An interferometer records how light interferes as a mirror moves, and the spectrum is then computed mathematically. For lunar work, the spectra are most useful when they show the Christiansen feature, a spectral maximum near 8 micrometres that is associated with silicate composition and particle size. The Lucy L'TES lunar spectra reported a Christiansen feature maximum near 8.15 micrometres (about 1,226 cm-1) [4]. A thermal instrument can also measure surface temperature directly, which is needed to interpret the emitted spectrum [5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a thermal emission spectrometer is to identify the materials at a planetary surface and to map their distribution. The Mars Global Surveyor TES investigation listed five objectives: the composition of surface minerals, rocks and ices; the temperature and dynamics of the atmosphere; the properties of atmospheric aerosols and clouds; the nature of the polar regions; and the thermophysical properties of surface materials [1]. For the Moon, the proposed application is orbital mapping of surface composition, which Nash and colleagues evaluated in 1993 for a polar-orbiting spacecraft [3]. The Lucy L'TES observations were described primarily as an in-flight calibration and validation target, with spectra consistent with Diviner orbital constraints and Apollo soil laboratory measurements [4][5].
article.operating_principle: Every object above absolute zero emits thermal radiation. The amount and spectral distribution of that emission depend on surface temperature and on emissivity, which is the efficiency with which a material emits compared with an ideal black body [5]. Silicate minerals have vibrational bands that absorb and emit strongly at particular infrared wavelengths, so their emission spectra show diagnostic features [3]. An interferometric spectrometer such as the MGS TES converts the interference record into a spectrum across the thermal infrared [1]. Retrieving emissivity requires separating temperature from emissivity, which the MAJIS analysis identifies as a central difficulty in the thermal-to-reflected crossover region [5].
article.scientific_importance: Thermal infrared spectroscopy addresses information that visible and near-infrared reflectance data cannot always supply. The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has provided near-global lunar surface temperature coverage since 2009 at roughly 200 metres per pixel [5]. A 2025 preprint analysis of JUICE MAJIS data notes that the 3.0 to 5.5 micrometre range, where reflected sunlight and thermal emission overlap, remains weakly covered at global scale [5]. Spectral measurements that extend into the thermal infrared, where the Christiansen feature occurs, therefore add a constraint that is not available from reflectance alone [4][5]. The Lucy L'TES observations were described by their authors as the first well-calibrated thermal infrared observations of the Moon at high spectral resolution [4]. Mars TES showed the value of this measurement type for global mineralogy and surface temperature mapping at another planet [1][10].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a thermal emission spectrometer. The examples below are a flown Mars instrument, a flown instrument that observed the Moon during a flyby whose hardware values could not be verified, a built lunar instrument whose mission was lost, and a 1993 proposed concept. The values should not be applied to other designs.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Only the MGS TES has a published enclosure size in the sources reviewed: 23.6 x 35.5 x 40.0 cm [1]; an ASU summary gives about 24 x 35 x 40 cm [2]. Dimensions for L'TES and the LTM instrument are not publicly specified. The 3.5 m figure in the Oxford announcement refers to the spacecraft with solar panels deployed, not to the instrument [7].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The MGS TES mass is 14.47 kg in the USGS summary [1] and about 14.4 kg in the ASU summary [2]. Mass for L'TES, the LTM and the 1993 concept is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. A 385 kg figure found on some JPL pages refers to a different Earth-observing instrument and was excluded from this article.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The USGS summary gives 10.6 W operating power for the MGS TES [1]; the ASU summary gives 14.5 W [2]. The conflict is disclosed rather than resolved. Power for the other examples is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A thermal emission spectrometer must keep its radiometric calibration while the surface and instrument undergo large temperature changes. Lunar day-night surface temperature contrasts are large, and Diviner's multi-year lunar temperature record was used to check the L'TES observations [4][5]. The MAJIS analysis shows that radiometric calibration errors and assumed surface reflectance can strongly affect thermal retrievals in the 3 to 5.5 micrometre crossover region [5]. The LTM's stated surface-temperature coverage of about -163 to 127 degrees Celsius describes the scientific mapping range, not a published instrument survival or operating limit [7]. No universal environmental requirement for a lunar thermal emission spectrometer is published in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: A thermal emission spectrometer measures emitted radiance, which combines surface temperature and emissivity. Separating the two requires assumptions about temperature, roughness and viewing geometry, and these assumptions can change the result in some wavelength regions [5]. Spectral features depend on particle size and mixing, so an emissivity spectrum does not give a unique composition [4]. Orbital mapping resolution is set by orbit, field of view and signal per pixel; the MGS TES mineralogy goal is a 3 km spatial resolution [1]. The lunar examples reviewed are a flyby observation, a lost mission and a 1993 concept, so no sustained lunar thermal emission mineral map from an operating spectrometer was found in this research [3][4][6].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A thermal emission spectrometer for the Moon would most likely be carried on an orbiting spacecraft, as the LTM was, or flown as a flyby instrument, as L'TES was. None of the examples reviewed was deployed on the lunar surface. Orbiter integration considerations include spacecraft integration, launch, cruise, orbit insertion, commissioning, pointing, thermal control and data interfaces [6][8][9].
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into the spacecraft on Earth. The LTM was installed on Lunar Trailblazer at Lockheed Martin Space in Colorado in 2023 [8][9].
Launch the spacecraft. Lunar Trailblazer launched on 26 February 2025 [6].
Transfer to the Moon and insert into orbit. For Lunar Trailblazer, operators lost contact the day after launch and orbit insertion was not reached [6].
Commission the instrument and spacecraft. Not achieved for Lunar Trailblazer [6].
Operate pointing, thermal and data interfaces for mapping. The LTM's interface requirements are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [7].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: No surface deployment method for a lunar thermal emission spectrometer is documented in the sources reviewed. The examples reviewed were carried on spacecraft: the MGS TES on a Mars orbiter [1][2], L'TES on the Lucy spacecraft during a lunar flyby [4][5], and the LTM on Lunar Trailblazer, a small lunar spacecraft whose solar panels fully deployed span about 3.5 m [6][7].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The MGS TES operated on a Mars orbiter [1][2]. L'TES observed the Moon during Lucy's 2022 Earth gravity assist [4][5]. The LTM was built and integrated for Lunar Trailblazer, which launched on 26 February 2025, lost contact, and was ended by NASA on 31 July 2025 [6][7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, orbiter or rover is asserted. Interface data (mass, power, data rate, pointing and thermal limits) were not verified for any lunar spacecraft. The Lunar Trailblazer launch vehicle and rideshare arrangement were not verified in this research, and the planned lander-led launch described in the 2023 Oxford announcement [7] was not used for compatibility assessment.

article.historical_significance: The 1993 Nash et al. study set out the case for mapping lunar composition from a polar orbit using thermal emission spectroscopy [3]. The MGS TES, a Mars instrument of this type, produced global surface temperature and mineralogy data, and its 1997 aerobraking temperature image illustrates the kind of product it generated [1][10]. In 2022, the Lucy L'TES observations of the Moon were described by their authors as the first well-calibrated, high-spectral-resolution thermal infrared spectra of the Moon [4]. The Lunar Trailblazer record states that the mission ended, with two-way contact never re-established, so no LTM lunar thermal data are reported [6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No thermal emission spectrometer is reported in these sources as operating in lunar orbit or on the lunar surface. Lucy L'TES evidence rests on an abstract-level summary and a secondary description in the MAJIS preprint [4][5]; the full paper and the instrument's mass, power, detector and field-of-view data were not verified. The MGS TES power value conflicts between the USGS summary (10.6 W) and an ASU summary (about 14.5 W) [1][2]. The LTM values come from a pre-launch announcement and are design intentions, not measured performance [7]. The Nash et al. (1993) concept has no flight heritage and no verified design specification [3]. Evidence gaps include L'TES hardware specifications, LTM wavelength range, detector type, mass and power, and any lunar thermal emission mineral map from an operating instrument.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Lucy L'TES hardware values (mass, dimensions, power, detector, field of view) were not verified. The SwRI instrument page returned a certificate error, and the Christensen et al. (2025) paper was read only through an abstract-level snippet on a mirror site. The 5.8-100 micrometre range comes from the MAJIS preprint's description of L'TES.

MGS TES power conflicts: USGS summary 10.6 W operating versus ASU summary about 14.5 W. The ASU summary was read from a search result, not a full page fetch. The USGS value is used as the primary figure and the conflict is stated in the article.

A 385 kg, 334 W, 650-3050 cm-1 specification appears on a tes.jpl.nasa.gov page. It describes a different Earth-observing instrument (reported in search results as the Aura Tropospheric Emission Spectrometer) and was excluded from the MGS TES values.

LTM values come from a pre-launch Oxford announcement dated 9 August 2023 and are design intentions. Wavelength range, detector type, mass and power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. A secondary summary described an uncooled microbolometer and a 7-10 micrometre narrowband range; these were not verified against a primary source and are not used.

Lunar Trailblazer launch vehicle and rideshare arrangement were not verified. The Oxford announcement's planned lander-led launch statement was superseded by the JPL record of a 26 February 2025 launch and was not used for any compatibility assessment.

Image verification: the PIA25831, PIA25837 and PIA00937 direct JPG URLs returned HTTP 206 image/jpeg on byte-range requests. The PIA25831 path with a /jpeg/ folder, suggested by a page summary, returned 404 and was not used. Full-resolution downloads were not checked. Reuse terms were not verified beyond the credit lines on the source pages.

No verified hardware photograph was found for MGS TES, L'TES or any lunar thermal emission spectrometer. The MGS image is a TES-derived temperature product. No L'TES image was included because none was verified.
Diviner (Paige et al., 2010) is cited as it appears in the MAJIS preprint and was not retrieved separately. Diviner is a lunar radiometer, not a spectrometer.
Christensen et al. (2025) journal publication status was not confirmed; the cited URL is a mirror site.
Mini-TES and the OSIRIS-REx OTES instrument were not researched and are outside the scope of this article.
No compatibility with a named lander, orbiter or rover is asserted. Lunar location recommendations are deferred by user instruction and are not included.
